excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: <@240180844130598912> I'm looking at the E2SS file structure and it looks to me like we only store state values at each block without the proofs. Is that correct, we don't store any MPT proofs?

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: Sorry not every block, I meant at specific block numbers

excerpts.author: milos88
excerpts.content:
E2SS stores entire snapshot of a state tree, at a given block.
Meaning, you can use it to recreate entire MPT trie, which you can use to create MPT proofs that you need.

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: I see, makes sense

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: So I guess it can't be used to reply the full state history then right? Because if some state gets created then deleted, or in the reverse order then the state snapshot won't have that data right?

excerpts.author: milos88
excerpts.content: yes, correct

excerpts.author: milos88
excerpts.content:
basically, we plan to use it in the following way:
1. initialize state bridge at a certain block (using e2ss)
2. execute blocks going forward and gossip state diffs
3. reach head of the chain, follow it, and gossip state diffs

steps 1 and 2 can be used for backfilling the state network as well

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: Ok interesting. I guess even just gossiping all the state from each state snapshot would put the majority of the state into the network anyway and then doing the execution and sending state diffs can fill in the gaps

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: I was thinking that I would be able to just execute the full history from these files initially, perhaps if they just contained the state diffs (new/updated state) at each block then that would be possible

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: Has anyone considered the state diff approach? Because in that case you could avoid the execution of the blocks when backfilling the historical state from these files

excerpts.author: milos88
excerpts.content:
There are tradeoffs. You could go and generate all state-diffs and put them in some e2store format (inluding the MPT proofs). Those files would probably be very big, but it would make bridges very simple.  And this only works for backfilling bridges.

If you want to follow the head of the chain or even to generate these files, you have to be able to execute blocks and create state-diffs. Executing blocks and creating state-diffs is relatively cheap (logic is not trivial, but it's not very expensive operation), so having a bridge do that doesn't seem like a big cost (i.e. gossiping the state-diff is much more expensive than generating state-diff).

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: True. Storing proofs for every block would make the files very large indeed and yes we will always need to execute in order to generate the files in the first place or to gossip the head the chain in real time. I see the files use case as just for seeding historical data and it is something very simple that anyone can simply download the files and run a bridge to contribute to seeding content into the network.

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: Actually we could have a file format that stores the state diffs without proofs for the entire state history. I think the file sizes would be more reasonable in that case. It would just require starting from genesis or from one of the E2SS state snapshots.

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: One downside of the state snapshots if that any two snapshots may contain duplicated state. For example the second state snapshot will likely contain much/most of the state that is in the first state snapshot. So if we regularly use the state snapshots to seed content then we may end up sending redundant state.

excerpts.author: b.hartnett
excerpts.content: Of course this would only happen if you seed all the state in the snapshot. If you only use the snapshot to initialize your local database before starting the execution then this is not a problem

excerpts.author: b.hartnett

Yes, that's correct
